title: Nane Ghat (नाणेघाट)
publisher: Marathi Vishwakosh / Maharashtra Rajya Marathi Vishwakosh Nirmiti Mandal
supports: Satavahana-period formation, Nane Ghat's ancient Desh–Konkan trade role, route between Junnar and Murbad, its position at Jivdhan, and Jivdhan's ability to control the pass.
caveat: Modern reference article, not a 1622 itinerary.

title: Gazetteer of the Bombay Presidency: Poona District, Trade and Communications
supports: Poona district historic roads and passes; Bor pass; Malsej-Ana pass road; Tamni/Sathpayri pedestrian footpath; the named ferry locations, routes, nineteenth-century service classes, seasons and establishment dates.
caveat: The described ferries are 19th-century services. 'Established before 1875' does not mean established by 1622; Tamni/Sathpayri is not conclusively equated with modern Tamhini.

title: Poona District Gazetteer, Places of Interest: Jivadhan Fort
date: 20th-century district gazetteer based on earlier district records
supports: Jivdhan described as commanding Nane Ghat; recorded as a Nizam Shahi fort until the dynasty's extinction and included in a Mughal transfer in 1637.
caveat: Does not establish exact 1622 killedar or the pass's daily traffic.

title: Malshej Ghat
publisher: District Administration, Thane, Government of Maharashtra
supports: Present Malshej location on the Kalyan–Nagar road and current route from Junnar via Narayangaon.
caveat: Present road alignment; not proof of a 1622 route.

title: Malshej Ghat
publisher: Department of Tourism, Government of Maharashtra
supports: Official tourism overview describes Malshej as a mountain pass, references historic strategic movements and old trade routes, and identifies Harishchandragad nearby.
caveat: General historical statement; no 1622 route date or operational details.

title: Shivneri and Junnar-area forts, Maharashtra Ahead
publisher: Directorate General of Information and Public Relations, Government of Maharashtra
supports: Modern description of Shivneri/Junnar and its surrounding route setting.
caveat: Tourism-oriented government magazine; not a direct 1622 route source.

title: The Imperial Gazetteer of India, Vol. II, entry 'Bhor Ghat'
supports: Bhor Ghat as a strategic Deccan gateway; pack-bullock traffic before road construction; artillery access improved in 1804; carriage road completed in 1830.
caveat: Retrospective nineteenth-century account; no direct 1622 road specification.

title: Lohagad and Visapur
supports: States Lohagad and Visapur guarded the Bor Ghat trade route; dates Visapur construction to 1713–1720.
caveat: Do not backdate Visapur to 1622; general tourism account does not specify the precise 1622 commanding arrangement.

title: Gazetteer of the Bombay Presidency: Ratnagiri and Savantvadi, Trade and Communications
date: late 19th century gazetteer; includes Captain Clunes' 1826 itinerary
supports: Kumbharli as the principal northern Ratnagiri pass to Dabhol/Chiplun; Clunes' 1826 description of the old pass as long, winding, rocky and then a major high road after repair.
caveat: Nineteenth-century description; no dated evidence for a 1622 pass commander or seasonal status.

title: Gazetteer of the Bombay Presidency: Satara District, Trade Roads
supports: Early trade routes to Konkan ports by Kumbharli and other passes; pass-network and fort relationships; later cart-road construction.
caveat: The source explicitly describes the early route as a retrospective inference; distinguish ancient/pre-modern use from exact 1622 operation.

title: Gazetteer of the Bombay Presidency: History of the Konkan, Section III
date: late 19th century gazetteer synthesizing earlier accounts
supports: A Bijapur–Dabhol route via Kumbharli and Chiplun's traffic; a later 1630s Shahji movement through a pass called Kumbha; early modern Deccan–Konkan trade.
caveat: Kumbha is not equated conclusively with Kumbharli; the Shahji episode is later than 1622. Route citation for Kumbharli is sourced through Ogilby and retrospective gazetteer synthesis.

title: Tamhini Ghat
publisher: Divisional Commissioner, Konkan Division, Government of Maharashtra
supports: Modern location reference for Tamhini Ghat near Mulshi and Mangaon.
caveat: Does not attest a premodern path or 1622 use.
